notes.decision: Translated 'foul.' From ⲃⲁⲓ̈ⲉ 'be foul, abominable,' the chapter's keyword (cf. accumulated vocab ⲛ̄ⲃⲁⲓ̈ⲉ). Capturing both physical disfigurement and the negative aesthetic-moral register that the laughter of bystanders implies.

Translated 'beautiful.' Lycopolitan circumstantial of ⲛⲉⲥⲉ 'be beautiful' (qualitative ⲛⲉⲥⲱⲥ/ⲛⲉⲥⲱⲩ); the final ϩ for ⲥ/ϥ is regular Lyc. orthography. The body/soul antithesis (foul body, beautiful soul) is the chapter's structuring contrast.
Translated 'even but in his soul.' ϩⲱϩ = Lyc 'also/even-himself' (cf. accumulated vocab); the restored ⲁⲉ = ⲇⲉ 'but' carries the contrastive force completing the antithesis of the chapter title.
Translated 'before him.' Lycopolitan ϩⲓ-ⲧⲉϩ-ϩⲏ 'in his front' = 'before him.' Same compound underlies ϩⲓⲧⲉϩⲏ 'before' in line 25 (without the possessive ϩ).
Translated 'humpbacked.' Coptic ⲕⲁⲕⲏⲡⲉ 'crippled, deformed' with epenthetic ϩ. Pairs with ⲗⲟⲩⲥⲉ 'maimed' as the standard physical-disfigurement doublet for the chapter's central figure.

Translated 'he is perfect.' Lycopolitan qualitative of ϫⲱⲕ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'be complete, perfect' (cf. accumulated ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲉⲧⲭⲏⲕ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'the Perfect Man'). Here the predicate of inner-spiritual completeness contrasted with bodily disfigurement.

Translated 'he prostrated.' From ϣⲱϣⲧ̄ 'stretch out, prostrate' (Lyc reduplicated/intensive form). The collocation with ⲁⲭⲙ̄ ⲡⲕⲁϩ 'upon the ground' confirms a prostration-of-worship gesture preceding the act of ⲟⲩⲱϣⲧ 'worship.'

Translated 'raising himself to give.' ⲧⲟⲛⲱ is the Lycopolitan variant of ⲧⲟⲩⲱ 'raise' (per terminology rule, vertical semantics preserved); ⲉϩⲧⲉⲁⲩ likely Lyc. ⲉ-ϯ + dative suffix 'to give them/him.' The elect, in his joy, raises himself up to render homage/praise.

Translated 'disturb.' Standard ϣⲧⲟⲣⲧⲣ̄ 'disturbance, agitation' (in accumulated vocabulary as ⲡⲥ̄ⲧⲣ̄ⲧⲣ̄). The laughter and mockery 'did not disturb' that elect — confirming the chapter's thesis: the inwardly-righteous one is unmoved by external derision.

Translated 'the Glorious One' per accumulated glossary entry. In context this is most likely the speaker (the apostle/Mani) of the kephalaion, who is then described embracing an elect disciple in lines 3-5.
ⲥⲁⲕϥ̄ ⲁⲣⲁϩ = 'drew him to himself' (ⲥⲱⲕ + ⲁⲣⲁϥ); ⲁⲗϩ = ⲱⲗϩ̄/ⲱⲗϫ 'embrace.' The sequence describes the Glorious One drawing the elect to himself and embracing him.
ⲧⲁⲟϩ = ⲧⲁϩⲟ 'set, place'; with ⲁⲍⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲡⲉϩⲥⲱⲙⲁ = 'set him within unto his body' — a tight embrace, body to body. ⲉϩⲭⲓ ⲡⲁⲥⲡⲁⲥⲙⲟⲥ = 'receiving the kiss.'
Greek εὐγενεῖς ('noble') and ἐλεύθεροι ('free') — the standing pair for high-status laity. The 'noble ones and free ones' constitute the assembly that has laughed at the humble disciple.

Read as ⲛⲁⲍⲣⲛ̄ⲧⲏⲛⲉ 'before you (pl.)' — Lycopolitan reflex of ⲛⲁϩⲣⲛ̄ + 2pl suffix, with directional ⲁ-. The faith dwells within him 'before/in the sight of you,' giving Mani's rebuke its force: even visibly so, you fail to discern.

ⲟ̄ⲁⲓⲉ taken per glossary as 'farmer' (Lyc. ⲟⲩⲁⲓⲉ = ⲟⲩⲱⲓⲉ). The phrase 'a man who is a farmer in his body' describes the disciple's humble outward form (laboring/cultivator station) — contrast with the inner Mind of Light. The image fits the Manichaean topos of the apostle disguised as cultivator. Alternative readings (e.g. ⲟⲩⲁⲉⲉⲧ⸗ 'alone') are formally possible but less supported by glossary.

Greek χήρα 'widow' — relativized 'who is widowed.' The widow-with-her-eaten-fruit is a parable image: the humble disciple is like a widow who has consumed her sustenance (perhaps her ⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ, the partly visible word at line-end), having nothing left of worldly resources, yet rich in prayer/fasting/humility.

Read 'a Youth, a small king, beautiful' — describing the inner divine presence within the outwardly humble old man. ⲗⲓⲗⲟⲩ = the Manichaean Christological 'Youth' (cf. glossary). The 'small king' indicates the indwelling royal-divine power hidden in humble form. ⲉⲛⲉⲥⲱⲥ qualitative of ⲉⲣⲉ-ⲛⲉⲥⲱ (= ⲛⲉⲥⲉ-) 'be beautiful.'

ⲥⲁⲓⲉ 'beauty' + ⲙⲛⲧⲍⲟⲩⲧⲉⲛ 'uprightness' (abstract from ⲥⲟⲩⲧⲱⲛ). ϣⲏⲗ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ tentative 'comes forth/emanates forth' — qualitative of an ⲁⲃⲁⲗ-compound verb of emergence. The beauty of uprightness emerges from within and is visible as the inner divine quality.

Per glossary, ⲡⲡⲣⲟⲧⲟⲙⲏ is the Third Ambassador's foremost-image (Greek προτομή). ⲧⲏⲟ̄ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ = ⲧⲁⲩⲟ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ qualitative 'sent forth.' The Protomē sent forth fits the cosmological background: the indwelling Mind of Light in the disciple is the manifestation of the Third Ambassador's icon. Continues into l.26 with feminine subject 'manifesting/revealing herself to you.'

notes.coptic_form: ⲡⲥⲍⲏⲧ ⲛⲁⲃⲓⲧⲏⲛⲉ ⲉⲛ ⲡⲉ ⲁⲥⲱⲃⲉ ⲛⲥⲁ ⲡⲓⲍⲗⲗⲟ
notes.decision: Negative cleft/predicate: 'It is not the heart that shall bring you to laugh at this old man' = 'the heart shall not in any way lead you to laugh at this old man.' ⲍⲗⲗⲟ = ϩⲗⲗⲟ 'old man' (Lyc. ⲍ for ϩ). The disciple addressed is now identified as ⲡⲓⲍⲗⲗⲟ — an elderly elect.

Quotation/paraphrase of Matthew 18:10: 'their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father.' Coptic ⲙⲙⲏⲛⲉ 'daily' renders the Greek διαπαντός. The Manichaean adaptation specifies ⲛⲓⲕⲟⲩⲓ̄ ⲙⲡⲓⲥⲧⲟⲥ 'the little faithful ones' — the humble elect — whose guardian angels behold the Father continually. This dominical citation grounds Mani's rebuke: laughing at the humble elect is sin against God Himself.
Parsed as 'ⲡⲁⲭⲉ-ⲩ ⲙ̄-ⲡⲫⲱⲥⲧⲏⲣ ⲛⲁⲩ' = 'the Illuminator said to them' — the duplicated dative -ⲩ/ⲛⲁⲩ is unusual but fits Lyc. discourse-introducer. Standard Kephalaia formula 'X said to them.'

Last visible letters before lacuna — start of an unidentified verb governing 'pearls.' Possibly ⲱⲑⲡ̄ 'be joined' or related; left transliterated 'ōth-' since the verb cannot be identified from these two letters alone. Context (the disciples' question about how pearls form) requires a verb of formation/coming-to-be.

Phonetic/scribal variant of ⲡⲗⲁⲥⲥⲉ 'mold/fashion' (Greek πλάσσειν), possibly with reduced gemination + vowel-doubling marking emphasis or scribal hesitation. The triple ⲉ̄ likely represents a stretched articulation. Translated as 'molded.'
Idiomatic doubled noun 'place place' = 'in certain places, place by place' — emphatic distributive construction contrasting with 'every place' / 'the entire sea.'

ⲣⲱⲭϩ̄ = 'burning' (cf. ⲣⲱⲭⲉ̂ in glossary), with feminine possessive ⲡⲉⲥ-. ⲃⲱϩⲧ̄ tentatively read as Lyc. variant of ⲡⲱϩⲧ̄ 'pour, gush' qualitative — fitting fire/heat 'gushing forth upward.' ⲃ for ⲡ is a known Lyc. orthographic alternation.
= ⲡⲧⲗⲧⲗ 'the dripping' (in glossary) — the descending drops of rain that constitute the parable's central image. The pearl-formation depends on this 'dripping' from above.

Qualitative form, taken as 'sweet' (Lyc. ϩⲁⲗⲟ ~ ϩⲗⲟϭ) — 'sweet waters' opposed to the salt sea, fitting the parable: rain-water (sweet) drops into the sea, and where it mingles with sweet pockets, pearls form.
= ⲡϣⲓⲭϩ/ⲡⲱⲓⲭⲍ 'abyss/depth' (in glossary). 'The depth of the sea' — the pearls do not go down to the abyss but stay in the upper sweet-water layer.

Tentatively read as 'shell/oyster' — the matrix that molds pearls. Possibly feminine variant of ⲧⲃⲧ 'fish' (in glossary) extended to mollusks, or related to ⲧⲱⲱⲃⲉ 'seal/imprint' (for the shell that imprints the pearl). Without clearer parallel left as 'shell.'

Qualitative 'being holy/pure' (Lyc. ⲟⲩⲁⲁⲃ → ⲟⲩⲁⲭ with regular ⲃ→ⲭ shift). Modifies 'the dripping' — the rain that forms pearls is characterized as holy, fitting the correspondential register where rain = descending light.
'She also, who makes a dripping of rain-water' — feminine subject (likely 'the sea' or 'the sweet water within the sea') is itself an active producer of dripping. ϩⲱⲱⲥ = Lyc. ϩⲱⲱⲥ 'also-she.'

Read as 'it is not (the case) that she is single.' ⲉⲙ = Lyc. negative ⲁⲛ; ⲉⲥⲟⲩⲁⲝ = circumstantial fem. 'while she is single' (cf. line 15 ⲧⲗ̄ⲧⲗⲉ ⲉⲥⲟⲩⲁⲝ 'a single drop'). The drop, although capable of being single, is here divided.

Read as Lyc. circumstantial 'while she is sweet/agreeable' from a root cognate with ϩⲗⲟϭ 'sweet' (cf. ⲁⲡⲭⲗⲥⲉ in vocabulary). The drop is described as sweet — fitting the rain/honey-drops register of cosmic descent imagery.

Read as a variant of ⲡⲙⲟⲩⲛϩⲱⲩ 'downpour' (in glossary) with sweetness-element ϩⲱⲗⲟ̄ (= ϩⲗⲟϭ 'sweet') incorporated, hence 'sweet rain/sweet downpour.' The compound parallels the ⲉⲥϩⲁⲗⲟ̄ 'sweet' qualification of the drops in line 2.
Read as conjunctive 'and they sink/dive in' from ϣⲱⲙⲥ 'submerge, dive' (cf. accumulated ⲁⲱⲙⲥ̄). The drops sink into the oyster after entering the sea — fits cosmographic-pearl imagery.
Parsed as habitual prefix ϣⲁⲥ- + ⲟ ('be') = 'she habitually is.' The relative ⲉⲧⲉϣⲁⲥⲟ ⲛ̄ϩⲃⲏⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ϣⲁⲣⲡ̄ = 'which habitually is a first oyster' — the qualifying class designation.

Read as conjunctive 'and they become great' — likely Lyc. ⲃⲱⲛ-ⲛⲁⲟ̄ = 'become great,' a compound of a stative-becoming verb with ⲛⲁⲟ̄ 'great.' The construction recurs in line 15 (ϣⲁⲥⲃⲟⲩⲛⲁⲟ̄) for the same 'becoming-great' of pearls.

ⲉⲓⲁⲟⲥ unidentified; tentatively rendered 'Iaos-gem.' Could be a kind of pearl, a Greek loan (cf. ἴασις, ἴαμα?), or a class of sea-stone. Recurs at line 20 ⲛⲁⲟ̄ ⲛⲉⲓⲁⲟⲥ 'great Iaos-gems.' Flagged for parallels.

Untranslated technical term ('the kek'). In context (lines 11, 28), ⲡⲝⲉⲕ is a class of formed thing in the oyster — possibly a coral, shell-substance, or stage of pearl-formation between rain-drop and full pearl. Distinct from ⲡⲝⲱⲃⲉ (line 29). Both are cause-stages in the chain rain → ⲡⲝⲱⲃⲉ → oyster → ⲡⲝⲉⲕ → pearl.
From root ⲟⲱⲭⲃⲉ 'be smaller, diminish' (in glossary). The construction ⲟⲩⲁⲛ ⲉϩⲁⲟ̄ⲱⲝⲃⲉ ⲁⲛⲉⲓ̈ = 'some that are smaller than these' — completing the gradation from many → fewer → smaller pearls.

Read here as positive existential 'when there is.' Glossary records ⲛⲉⲕⲁⲟⲛ/ⲉⲕⲁⲟⲛ as 'is not / there is not,' but this Lyc. form may function in both polarities depending on context. The positive sense fits the parallel structure ⲡ̄ⲥⲁⲡ ⲙⲉⲛ ('on one occasion') with subsequent ⲉⲣⲉ ⲧⲗ̄ⲧⲗⲉ ⲥⲛ̄ⲧⲉ in line 17.

Read as scribal/dialectal variant of ⲧⲃⲏⲧⲉ 'oyster' (ϩ for ⲃ). Context demands the same referent as ⲧⲃⲏⲧⲉ throughout: the drop is received and forms a pearl. Alternative reading 'the inner-part/heart' is less compelling given the immediate parable.

Possessed feminine noun 'her splendor/beauty.' ⲉⲥⲟⲩ likely related to ⲉⲥⲱ 'be beautiful' or ⲥⲟⲩ 'value, time/moment.' In conjunction with ⲝⲏⲕ 'complete,' the sense is 'her splendor/perfection is complete.'
Standard Coptic ⲁⲓⲧⲥⲁⲃⲉ-ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ 'I have taught you (pl.)' in Lyc. orthography. This is the chapter-summary formula: the Apostle declaring what he has just shown.

Read as 'the divers' — Lycopolitan rendering of Greek κολυμβηταί (pearl-divers), with ⲝ for κ. Fits the parable's conclusion: divers gather pearls from the sea-places and bring them up in myriads. Confidence moderate; the lexeme is otherwise unattested in this form.
Read as Greek μυριάς 'myriad,' fitting the aggregate context of pearls being brought up from the sea by divers. Alternative reading as proper name (Maria) is contextually impossible here.

Ending of ⲙⲁⲣⲅⲁⲣⲓⲧⲏⲥ 'pearls' (Greek μαργαρίτης) whose first portion stood on the prior page (203). Confirmed by occurrence of ⲍⲙⲙⲁⲣⲅⲁⲣⲓ-ⲧⲏⲥ split across lines 18-19. Translated as 'pearls' (parenthetical) since the rest of the word is on the previous page.
Lycopolitan reflex of Greek κολυμβητής 'diver' (with regular Lyc. ⲭ for κ). The pearl-diving parable is a known Manichaean trope. ⲅⲓⲛⲉ = Greek γίνε(ται) 'becomes (active), takes effect.'

Translated as 'wells, depths' from Coptic ϣⲁⲧⲉ/ϣⲱⲧⲉ 'pit, well.' In line 12 these are equated with the φωστῆρες (luminaries = sun and moon ships of Manichaean cosmology). The diving wells thus correspond to the gathering-points of cosmic Light.

ⲛ̄ⲡⲣⲁⲓ̈ = 'the kings' (Lyc. plural of ⲣ̄ⲣⲟ/ⲡⲟⲣⲟ, accumulated vocabulary). ⲙⲙⲉⲣⲓⲥⲧⲁⲛⲟⲥ = Greek μεγιστάνες 'magnates, grandees.' Standard Manichaean court-imagery extended cosmically: the kings and magnates of the parable correspond to the Aeons of Greatness (line 13).

Translated as 'the shell' contextually. Pairs with ⲧⲃⲏⲧⲉ 'date-palm' as the two natural hosts to which the flesh of humanity is likened — the date-palm bears fruit (souls), the shell holds the pearl (soul). Etymology uncertain; possibly Lyc. for a shell/casing term. Confidence moderate.

Greek ἁρπαγή 'plundering, snatching' + Coptic verb ⲧⲱⲣⲡ̄ 'snatch' (in glossary). Cognate-object construction: 'the plundering itself which they snatch (her).' The pearl, snatched from the oyster's casing, is here the typological correspondent of the soul taken from the flesh.

Tentatively rendered 'casing' as the casing/case of the oyster. Could be Greek θήκη 'case, sheath' through dialectal phonological adaptation, or a Lycopolitan term for shell/integument. The function is to name the oyster's shell-coverign that breaks open to release the pearl. Confidence moderate.

Plural ⲙ̄ⲫⲱⲥⲧⲏⲣ 'luminaries' (Greek φωστῆρες) — the two great luminaries of Manichaean cosmology, sun and moon. The wells of the parable correspond to the cosmic luminary-ships that gather and convey light upward.
Direct address: 'You yourselves, my beloved ones.' ⲍⲱⲧⲧⲏⲛⲉ = Lyc. intensive 'yourselves' (in glossary); ⲛⲁⲙⲉⲣⲉⲧⲉ = 'my beloved (ones)' (1sg poss. + plural of ⲙⲉⲣⲓⲧ).

Read as 'hear the saying of every form' or 'the word in every manner.' ⲥⲱⲭⲉ = Lyc. ϣⲁϫⲉ 'word, saying' (cf. accumulated ⲥⲉⲭⲉ 'word/saying'). Functions here either as imperative 'hear!' or as nominative substantive — the saying being interpreted is the parable. Translated 'hear the saying' for clarity.

Greek ἀρχιέμπορος 'chief-merchant.' Capitalized as a divine cosmic figure: the great Chief-Merchant who receives the pearl-souls retrieved by the diver-apostles. Standard Manichaean apostolic-merchant typology (cf. accumulated vocabulary on ⲡⲉϩⲛⲁⲃ ⲛⲉⲟⲩⲉⲓⲛ 'his vessels of import' and ⲙⲛⲧⲓⲉⲡϣⲱⲧ 'merchant trade').
